newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe opposition launches court battle on laws.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe opposition launches court battle on laws.

text.p: An opposition Party launched a court battle on Wednesday to have some provisions of Zimbabwe's electoral rules scrapped.

The United Parties (UP) filed a motion with the Supreme Court demanding that it declare unconstitutional an act which has allowed President Robert Mugabe's ZANU-PF to be the only party drawing state funding and a provision banning amendments to the voters roll once a poll date has been set.
Under the 1992 Political Parties Finance Act, only parties with a minimum of 15 seats in the 150-member parliament are eligible to receive financial help from public coffers.

ZANU-PF, which has been in power since Zimbabwe gained independence in 1980, has 147 seats and has been the only one receiving the allocation which started with Z$32 million (US$2.8 million) in 1993 and has risen to an estimated Z$65 million in the 18-month budget announced last Thursday.
"Once you have the principle of public funding of political activity then the concept of equality is vital," advocate Adrian de Bourbon, representing the UP, told the court.
The UP boycotted presidential elections last year citing electoral rules which it said favoured ZANU-PF.

"Where you have legislation which impinges on the right to vote it impinges on the freedom of expression and the democratic rights guaranteed under the Constitution. To have a provision which precludes any attempt to rectify voters rolls is not reasonably justifiable in a democratic society," de Bourbon said.
The five-member court is expected to rule on the motion in September.

Attorney-General Patrick Chinamasa, whose office is cited as one of the respondents, told the court the criteria for provision of state funding for political parties should be left to the legislature to decide.

"Putting it (the threshold) at 15 seats made it impossible for any other party to obtain funding...We have to try and make the playing field level," Chief Justice Anthony Gubbay said after Chinamasa argued that anyone entering politics should start from scratch and build up a following to qualify for state funding.
Justice Nicholas McNally said a system of political funding based on the number of voters for each party was more reasonable.
"With the criteria using the number of members of parliament, the more I think about it the more I cannot see its relevance," the judge said.
